# Language principles

BasedPL (BPL) keeps APL's glyphs and its right-to-left evaluation. It changes the notation where APL's rules make code harder to read or to write. Most of the changes follow from one decision: lists are written in brackets. The array model comes from BQN. The name BasedPL stands for Based-array Programming Language, after that model. Many of the notation choices answer problems that Marshall Lochbaum, BQN's author, lists in his notes on [BQN's problems](https://mlochbaum.github.io/BQN/commentary/problems.html) and on [its first five years](https://mlochbaum.github.io/BQN/commentary/fiveyears.html). [Shared language rules](rules.qmd) states the rules without the reasons. [BPL, APL and BQN side by side](comparison.qmd) shows the choices on real code.

## Lists are written in brackets

In APL, arrays written side by side form a list. `1 2 3` is a vector, and so are `a b c` and `(x+1) y`. This is called stranding. It is short, but it gives a space a different job in different places. Between arrays, a space separates the items of a list. Between functions, it means nothing. `+/÷≢` and `+ / ÷ ≢` are the same train. Between an operator and an array, it can do either.

That last case causes real trouble. An operator's right operand is the single item to its right, and stranding happens first. In APL, the operand in `f⍤1 M` is `1 M`. You have to write `f⍤1⊢M`, where `⊢` is there only to break the strand. BQN's documentation gives the example `a +˝∘×⎉1‿∞ b`, a matrix product. No rule decides well which of `1`, `∞` and `b` should strand together. BQN marks its strands with `‿` instead.

In BPL, lists are written in brackets, `[a b c]`, as in Python and JavaScript. Lochbaum notes that new BQN programmers "are always expecting `[]` to be the list notation, and it'd let you copy-paste JSON too". A list of literals can still leave its brackets out. `1 2 3` and `"no" "yes"` are vectors. Arrays side by side also form a list. `a b` is `[a b]`.

```bpl
x←5
[1 x 3]              ⍝ 1 5 3
≢[+/ ÷ ≢]            ⍝ 3ₓ
```

Subjects side by side always form a strand, whatever the names hold. `(+/x) 3` is a two-item list whether `x` is a vector or a matrix. Selection uses [Index](glyphs/squad.qmd), `⌷`. Each run is one item of the strand. For example, `a b+1` is `[a (b+1)]`, and `[1 2] 3` is `[[1 2] 3]`.

A bracket list is always a vector, whatever the number of items. `[1 2 3]` is `1 2 3`, and `[1]` is a one-item vector. A single literal isn't a strand: `1` is a number.

Parentheses only group, as they do in maths. `(1+2)×3` is 9, `(1 2)` is `1 2`, and `(x)` is `x`. `⊂[1 2]` is a scalar holding a vector, as in BQN. `⊂+` is a train, not a scalar. `+ᵘ` is a scalar holding `+`.

```bpl
⍴[1]                 ⍝ [1]ₓ
⍴⊂[1 2]              ⍝ ⍬ₓ
(1+2)×3              ⍝ 9
```

Array notation extends brackets to higher ranks. `[1 2 ⋄ 3 4]` is a matrix, as in Dyalog's array notation. The rows between `⋄` become major cells, and the result has one more axis than each row. `[1 ⋄ 2]` is the vector `1 2`, because its rows are numbers. `[[1] ⋄ [2]]` is a column, because its rows are one-item vectors. `[a ⋄ b]` is the Mix of `[a b]` when `a` and `b` have the same shape.

A vector of rows is written in parentheses, with `⋄` between the rows. The rows can differ in length. Each row is a vector, as if written in brackets. Rows inside brackets form a new axis, and rows inside parentheses form a new level of nesting. A row holding one string is still a one-item vector: `("ab" ⋄ "cd")` is `[["ab"] ["cd"]]`. The vector of strings is written `["ab" "cd"]`, and the vector of names `[x y]`.

```bpl
(4 ⋄ 4 5 ⋄ 4 5 6)≡[[4] [4 5] [4 5 6]]   ⍝ $t
≢¨(1 2 ⋄ 3)                            ⍝ [2 1]ₓ
```

Items in brackets can be functions. `[+/ ÷ ≢]` is a vector of three functions, and `[+/÷≢]` is a one-item vector holding the mean function. Writing a function expression in brackets is therefore one way to make it a value. BQN needs `⊑⟨Expr⟩` or a name for this, which Lochbaum lists under "Converting a function expression to a subject is tricky". The other way is `fᵘ`, a scalar holding the function `f`.

Items in a list are evaluated left to right, as statements are. BQN chose the same order for its lists and strands.

## Spaces group

Outside brackets, literals separated by spaces form a strand, as in `1 2 3`. Every other space separates runs. A run is a sequence of tokens with no spaces between them. Each run is evaluated first, and then the runs combine. Spaces act as light parentheses.

```bpl
a←1 ⋄ b←2 ⋄ c←3 ⋄ d←4
a+b×c+d              ⍝ 15
a+b × c+d            ⍝ 21
```

Runs also fix the operand problem. Because a run ends at a space, `f⍤1 M` applies rank 1 to `M` with no `⊢`. A literal argument would still join the operand's strand. For example, `f⍤1 2 3` has the operand `1 2 3` and no argument. Write a literal vector argument in brackets, as in `f⍤1[2 3]`. A run that ends in a dyadic operator takes the next run as its right operand, as if no space came between them. `f⍤ 1 M` therefore means `f⍤1 M`. A space after an operator also lets a longer function be its operand without parentheses: `⌊⌾ 10× x`.

```bpl
m←2 3⍴⍳6
+/⍤1 m               ⍝ 3 12
+/⍤ 1 m              ⍝ 3 12
+/⍤1(2 3⍴⍳6)         ⍝ 3 12
```

Lochbaum describes the problem that runs solve, under "Modifiers look looser than trains without spaces". In BQN's `⋆∘-×˜`, the `-` looks closer to `⋆`, but it binds to `×˜`. Writing `⋆∘- ×˜` shows the structure. He calls it "unfortunate that this is something the writer must do rather than something the notation encourages". In BPL the space is part of the notation. Under "Long trains are hard for humans to parse", he notes that readers lose track of a train's structure after four to eight parts. Runs let spaces show that structure: `⌊ +/÷≢` is the floor of the mean.

Code that is fully spaced, or not spaced at all, groups as in APL. Only mixed spacing changes the grouping. A reader used to APL reads `1+2 × 3` as 7, and here it is 9. A tool that normalises spaces would change a program's meaning.

Other languages give spaces meaning too. K reads `a -1` differently from `a - 1`. Nim tried an experimental mode in which the spaces around an operator changed its precedence, and removed it in version 0.20.

## A run that ends in a function is a train

A run that ends in a function has no argument yet. It is a function, built as an APL train with one addition. A subject directly before a function binds to it. `2×` is `2⍃×`, and `32+1.8×` converts Celsius to Fahrenheit.

```bpl
f←32+1.8×
f100                 ⍝ 212
```

The rest follows APL's train rules, including Dyalog's fork with a subject on the left, `0.5×⊢+÷`. Binding covers the common case of fixing a left argument, without `⍃`. K has the same idea, called projection, in which `2*` is a function.

`+/÷≢ x` and `+/÷≢x` differ only in the space before `x`. `+/÷≢ x` is the train `+/÷≢` applied to `x`, which is the mean. `+/÷≢x` is one run that ends in a subject. It is an expression, `+/(÷(≢x))`.

```bpl
x←1 2 3 6
+/÷≢ x               ⍝ 3
+/÷≢x                ⍝ 1r4
```

If both spellings meant the same, the space would mean nothing. In everyday arithmetic the two readings agree. When the functions have arrays between them, as in `32+1.8×`, the train gives the same result as the expression. The readings differ only where a fork gets a function as its left part, as in `0.5×⊢+÷`. APL has the same split, with nothing in the source to mark it. Removing the argument from APL's `0.5×⊢+÷⍵` turns it into a fork with a different meaning. In BPL the space shows which reading you get.

## Selection is a function

Index, `⌷`, selects: `I⌷Y` takes one item of `I` for each leading axis of `Y`. In K, `v 1` selects, because K treats a list as a function of its positions. BPL keeps subjects and functions apart. Selection is a function like any other, and `v 1` is a strand. For one position, `1⌷v` is as long as `v 1`, and a [subscript](scripts.qmd#subscripts) is shorter: `v₁` is `1⌷v`.

Selecting with a number drops that axis from the result. Selecting with an array of positions puts the array's shape in place of the axis. `1⌷v` is an item, `[⊂1]⌷v` is a scalar holding that item, and `[[1]]⌷v` is a one-item vector. Dyalog has the same rule, but its `v[1]` looks like a one-item list and gives a scalar. A one-item result needs `v[,1]`.

```bpl
v←10 20 30 40
[[2 0]]⌷v            ⍝ 30 10
¯1⌷v                 ⍝ 40
1⌷v                  ⍝ 20
[⊂1]⌷v               ⍝ ⊂20
[[1]]⌷v              ⍝ [20]
```

Because Index takes its positions on the left, the array on its right can be any expression. `"NY"⌷+/sales` totals each row, then selects the row for NY, with no parentheses.

## Counting from 0

Positions and axes count from 0, as in BQN, J, K, Python and NumPy. Negative positions count from the end.

- A Boolean is a valid position, as in `c⌷"no" "yes"`. With 1-origin, the position would be `1+c`.
- Positions run from `¯n` to `n-1` with no gap. With 1-origin, position 0 is an error that sits between the first item and the last.
- `n|i` wraps a position round a vector of length `n`. `⌊i÷n` and `n|i` give the row and column of a flat position.
- The Python API returns positions from functions such as `grade` and `where`. Those positions must agree with Python and NumPy, which count from 0.

Counting idioms pay for this with a `1+`, as in `1+⍳10` for the numbers 1 to 10. Code from APL books and libraries assumes 1-origin and needs converting.

Two rules follow J and BQN where 0-origin left a choice. A negative length counts down, as J's `i._3` does. Interval Index counts the boundaries at or below each value, as BQN's does. Below the first boundary the count is 0. A position there would be `¯1`, which selects the last item.

```bpl
⍳¯3                  ⍝ 2 1 0
1 3 5⍸0 3 9          ⍝ [0 2 3]ₓ
```

## Based arrays

BPL uses BQN's [based array model](https://mlochbaum.github.io/BQN/doc/based.html). Numbers, characters and functions are atoms. An array is a rectangular collection of values, and an atom is not an array. Enclosing always adds a layer. `⊂3` is a rank-0 array holding 3, and it differs from 3.

```bpl
⊂3 ≡ 3               ⍝ $f
≡⊂⊂3                 ⍝ 2ₓ
```

APL's nested array model identifies a simple scalar with its enclosure, and enclosing 3 gives 3 again. Under the based model, every value has one representation, whether you pass it to a function, return it, or store it in an array. Functions are atoms too, and they can be items of a list, as in `[+/ ÷ ≢]`. Lochbaum's page on the model gives the longer argument.

## Functions act on major cells

BPL follows BQN's leading-axis model. A function that works on a whole array acts on its major cells, the cells along its first axis. The last-axis glyphs `⌽ / \ ,` are the leading-axis functions applied at rank 1, and their first-axis twins `⊖ ⌿ ⍀ ⍪` are the leading-axis functions themselves. Every function therefore treats a matrix by the same rule.

Search follows the same rule. `⍳ ∊ ~ ∪ ∩` compare the major cells of the searched argument. For a matrix, those are its rows. The other argument's cells have the same rank. A unit has no major cells to search. `s~" "` removes the spaces from a string, and `s~' '` is a `RANK` error.

Partition splits along the first axis too, into blocks of major cells. `⊂⍤1` splits each row instead, and `⊂⍠1` splits a matrix into blocks of columns. Encode and Decode put digits on the last axis, as J's `#:` and `#.` do. Encoding a vector gives one row of digits for each number, and Decode reads each row back.

```bpl
m←[1 2 ⋄ 3 4 ⋄ 1 2]
m~[1 2 ⋄ 5 6]          ⍝ [3 4 ⋄]
1 0 1⊂m                ⍝ [[1 2 ⋄ 3 4] [1 2 ⋄]]
2 2 2⊤5 6              ⍝ [1 0 1 ⋄ 1 1 0]
2⊥[1 0 1 ⋄ 1 1 0]      ⍝ 5 6
```

Rank 0 passes each 0-cell as a unit: an atom arrives as itself, and an array item arrives enclosed. BQN's `⎉0` encloses atoms as well. As a result, `⊢⍤0` returns its argument unchanged, even when the argument is nested. A function under `⍤0` also sees the same numbers that literals and selection give. Each, `¨`, is the operator that passes items.
